subject: software-engineering
name: Software Engineering
exam: TU assessment: 60% final examination set by the university, 40% internal (assignments, lab work, attendance).

units.title: Introduction to Software Engineering
topics: Software failures, real photographs and the cost of change

sections.title: Software failures, real photographs and the cost of change

summary: Software is more than code, and comes in system, application, embedded, web and AI forms; it can be generic or custom.
Good software is maintainable, dependable, efficient and acceptable.
Software engineering is a systematic engineering approach to the whole life cycle; it sits inside the broader field of system engineering.
Costs are dominated by maintenance and testing; major challenges are heterogeneity, change, security, scale and delivery time.
Professional practice demands competence, confidentiality and public-interest ethics.

units.title: Software Development Process Models
topics: Process iteration: incremental delivery and spiral
Pictures of the process models, and the people behind them

sections.title: Process iteration: incremental delivery and spiral
Pictures of the process models, and the people behind them

summary: All software processes contain specification, development, validation and evolution.

Plan-driven models (waterfall) suit stable requirements; iterative models (evolutionary, incremental, spiral, RUP) accommodate change; agile methods (Scrum, XP) and RAD give speed at the price of documentation.
CBSE builds from existing components; prototyping reduces requirement risk.
CASE tools support all phases but do not replace sound engineering.

units.title: Software Requirement Analysis and Specification
topics: Requirements in pictures: a lesson from the year 2000

sections.title: Requirements in pictures: a lesson from the year 2000

summary: Requirements are written at user and system levels and divided into functional, non-functional and domain requirements.
Elicitation uses viewpoints, interviews, scenarios, use cases and ethnography, followed by prioritisation and negotiation.
Validation uses reviews, prototypes and test-case writing to catch errors early.
The SRS records the agreed requirements in a standard structure; the feasibility study decides whether to proceed.

units.title: Software Design
topics: Design in pictures: people, patterns and diagrams

sections.title: Design in pictures: people, patterns and diagrams

summary: Design concepts (abstraction, modularity, information hiding, refinement, functional independence) aim at modules with high cohesion and low coupling.
Architectural styles organise the system: repository, client-server, layered, MVC; modules are decomposed by objects or functions.
Structured design maps DFDs to structure charts by transform or transaction analysis, with fan-in/fan-out metrics and pseudo-code for the detail.
UI design follows HCI principles; the choice of interaction style and presentation depends on users and tasks, and is validated by evaluation.

units.title: Coding
topics: Coding in pictures: from punched cards to code review

sections.title: Coding in pictures: from punched cards to code review

summary: Language and tool selection depends on problem, performance, team skill, platform, ecosystem and cost.
Good code follows a standard, uses clear names, is short and cohesive, handles errors, and is reviewed and tested.
LOC and Halstead measures describe size and effort but must be interpreted with care.

units.title: Software Testing and Quality Assurance
topics: Testing in pictures: from the first bug to the V-model

sections.title: Testing in pictures: from the first bug to the V-model

summary: Verification checks conformance to the specification; validation checks fitness for the user's needs. Inspections are the most cost-effective defect finders.
Black-box tests (equivalence classes, boundaries) come from the specification; white-box tests from the structure; cyclomatic complexity gives the minimum number of independent-path tests.
Testing proceeds from units to integration, system and acceptance (alpha, beta), with regression testing after every change.
Quality management combines product and process quality, measured by reliability numbers and improved through ISO 9001 and CMM maturity levels.

units.title: Software Maintenance
topics: Maintenance in pictures: old machines, new demands

sections.title: Maintenance in pictures: old machines, new demands

summary: Used software must evolve; ignoring evolution causes decay (Lehman's laws).
Maintenance is corrective, adaptive, perfective or preventive, with most effort spent on new or changed functionality, not on fixing faults.
Maintenance is costly, and effort can be estimated from annual change traffic; re-engineering or replacement is chosen by comparing value and cost.
Configuration management with baselines, versions and controlled change keeps releases reproducible and traceable.

units.title: Managing Software Projects
topics: Management activities and the need for management
Project management in pictures: estimates, networks and earned value

sections.title: Management activities and the need for management
Project management in pictures: estimates, networks and earned value

summary: Software projects are hard to manage because the product is intangible, one-off and changing; management comprises planning, scheduling, costing, monitoring, people and risk.
COCOMO and function points give effort estimates from size or functionality; they are uncertain and should be re-run as knowledge grows.
CPM finds the critical path and slack; PERT turns three-point estimates into probabilities of meeting a deadline; EVM measures real progress with CPI and SPI and forecasts the final cost.
Risk is managed by ranking exposure; people and communication determine more projects than tools do.
